title: Hybrid connectivity, NAT edge-cases & Private VPC deep dive
summary: Deep technical session on running Redwood Private in a hybrid VPC with restrictive NAT/egress policies. Main concerns: PrivateLink connectivity, DNS resolution for model pulls, path MTU and UDP edge cases, KV cache consistency across AZs, batching latency tradeoffs with MTU/NAT timeouts, and quantization CPU/GPU startup impacts. Agreed to run a 3-node pilot with simulated NAT timeouts and share an annotated network diagram + runbook.
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for carving out an hour. this is Lena from Redwood, i'm the account lead. marco and jules are here for the deep dive.
[00:12] Amir Khan: morning, thanks. we'll keep notes— i'm amir, platform eng. we've got a pretty locked-down setup at Sable. egress is via NAT gateway, only whitelisted endpoints.
[00:25] Marco Ortiz: got it. quick question— are you planning to use PrivateLink or site-to-site vpn into our VPC? those have different port/timeout characteristics.
[00:34] Priya Rao: PrivateLink ideally, we want no internet egress for model traffic. but we also have workloads that reach out for model downloads initially.
[00:44] Lena Park: good. we'll talk model pulls vs runtime inference. model pull can be done over a controlled path, or we can pre-push into your private registry.
[00:55] Derek Liu: on the nat side, our current timeout for ephemeral ports is 120s, but we've seen some long-lived connections drop earlier under load. curious how long the Redwood runtime keeps model shards streaming.
[01:12] Jules Meyer: runtime opens multiple connections during shard download and then long-lived grpc/tcp for inference depending on setup; for hosted->vpc connectivity via PrivateLink traffic is over AWS private endpoints, but for model onboarding initial pulls may go out.
[01:28] Amir Khan: right, so we need to avoid accidental internet egress. our security team will only whitelist the endpoint IPs they see; they don't want to open wide cidr blocks.
[01:38] Marco Ortiz: understood. one pattern we've used is egress through a centralized NAT with service-specific SNAT pools so the security team can correlate. for PrivateLink you can create interface endpoints per service and keep everything internal— but note that cross-AZ traffic and DNS resolution can surprise people.
[01:57] Priya Rao: what surprises?
[02:00] Marco Ortiz: two things: split-horizon DNS where the private route53 name resolves to different ips inside vs outside, and path MTU blackholes when tunnels are in play. also, PrivateLink endpoints have ENIs in subnets— if your subnets are too small you'll run out of ENI capacity.
[02:18] Derek Liu: we have /24s in prod subnets, but dev is smaller. ENI counts have bit us before.
[02:25] Lena Park: we'll include an ENI sizing guidance sheet in the doc we share. also note that KV cache traffic is local to the runtime but if you have a multi-AZ cluster we call out cross-AZ cache miss bandwidth.
[02:40] Amir Khan: sorry quick Q — "KV cache" in your docs, is that per-worker RAM or shared network cache?
[02:46] Jules Meyer: primarily per-worker local prefix/KV cache so hot prefixes don't require re-computation; we also support optional shared Redis backed cache for very large deployments, but that adds latency and an operational component.
[02:58] Priya Rao: can you quantify the cross-AZ penalty?
[03:02] Marco Ortiz: ballpark a 2-4 ms extra RTT when hitting another AZ in the same region, but if you saturate links or hit NAT throughput limits it can be higher, like 10-20 ms. that can matter at 50ms SLOs.
[03:18] Amir Khan: okay, 10-20ms is unfortunate. our p99 target is 75ms so anything above 10-15ms extra eats the buffer.
[03:27] Lena Park: that's why we do batching + async prefix caching. large batches can amortize network overhead but increase tail latency.
[03:36] Derek Liu: we currently have strict flow logs and NAT logging; would Redwood need to open many ephemeral ports? our security team will require a mapping.
[03:46] Marco Ortiz: the runtime multiplexes requests over a small pool of outbound sockets for model download and telemetry; for inference you mainly see inbound connections to a private endpoint. the model-downloader will use multiple concurrent ranges when pulling shards for speed—we can throttle that to fit your NAT capacity.
[04:05] Priya Rao: can you slow it down so we don't blow NAT ephemeral pools?
[04:08] Jules Meyer: yes, we have downloader concurrency knobs and backoff settings; we can stage shard pulls across a maintenance window.
[04:15] Amir Khan: DNS— we use a private resolver chain; when a name is registered with PrivateLink the route53 private zone is expected. any gotchas?
[04:24] Marco Ortiz: make sure your resolver supports EDNS properly and doesn't rewrite TTLs; we've seen some on-prem resolvers that strip DNS flags causing longer time to live glitches which delay failover. also mTLS to control plane vs data plane sometimes uses different names so double-check.
[04:44] Derek Liu: we had an incident where our split-horizon returned an external ip for the PrivateLink name because of stale delegation records.
[04:52] Lena Park: we'll add a diagnostic DNS checklist— capture dig + trace to see which resolver path is used.
[04:59] Priya Rao: cool. on quantization: our models are int8, we want to keep quality. any perf hit on cold start?
[05:08] Jules Meyer: quantized models typically have smaller memory footprint and faster per-token decoding, but the runtime may need to run a short fusing step and load quant tables—cold start can add 150-400ms depending on model size and disk speed. for warm replicas that's negligible.
[05:28] Amir Khan: so for p99 we need warm workers. does Redwood support pre-warming?
[05:32] Marco Ortiz: yes, you can pin minimum replicas and use a warm pool. our Dedicated/Private mode supports minimum-capacity configs.
[05:40] Derek Liu: about MTU— we use an IPSEC tunnel to an on-prem colo sometimes and we've hit TCP MSS/MTU blackholes causing fragmentation and slow downs. any recommendations?
[05:50] Jules Meyer: set path MTU discovery on the tunnel and prefer TCP MSS clamping on the VPN. also avoid UDP for large shard transfers; use TCP with congestion management.
[06:02] Amir Khan: curious about batching config. we have variable request sizes, sometimes short chat turns very bursty—how to keep latency low?
[06:11] Marco Ortiz: adaptive batching is the trick: small-size fast path with micro-batches for low latency, and a slower large-batch when throughput is the priority. you tune max_batch_size and max_wait_ms. the tradeoff: larger max_batch gives higher throughput and better GPU utilization, but increases median and tail latency.
[06:30] Priya Rao: any heuristics to pick batch sizes?
[06:33] Jules Meyer: start with target 10-20 tokens typical, set max_wait 5-10ms for chat, and increase if you see underutilization. we'll run load tests to find the knee for your request distribution.
[06:47] Derek Liu: do timeouts from NAT cause inflight request failures during batching?
[06:52] Marco Ortiz: only if the NAT times out during long RPCs; batching adds small delays, not long-lived idles. but if you have aggressive connection tracking on an intermediate firewall, it's possible during large model downloads.
[07:05] Amir Khan: action— can we test with our NAT session timeout set to 30s and 120s to see failure modes?
[07:11] Lena Park: yes, we'll simulate both; we'll provide a test harness script.
[07:15] Priya Rao: what monitoring do you expose for these network metrics?
[07:19] Marco Ortiz: we export per-route latency, socket errors, connection churn, and cache hit rate. Console has dashboards and traces.
[07:27] Amir Khan: great. a security question: KMS integration for model encryption at rest—do you support customer-managed keys?
[07:35] Jules Meyer: yes, Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM, bring-your-own-key is supported and we emit audit logs for key ops.
[07:42] Derek Liu: do audit logs flow over the same private links? we need them to hit our logging collector via private routes.
[07:49] Marco Ortiz: they can be forwarded via your VPC endpoints to your logging sinks; we also support push via a connector if you want.
[07:58] Priya Rao: about on-prem edge: we have some inference in colo with limited egress, using a small NAT pool and BGP. can Redwood runtime run fully on-prem with occasional control plane talk?
[08:10] Lena Park: yes, Private supports an on-prem package; control plane can be tunneled out via a small persistent connection or via a bastion with periodic pulls—depends on your compliance.
[08:22] Amir Khan: what's the fallback if control plane connectivity drops?
[08:25] Marco Ortiz: local serving keeps running for pinned model versions; you can't onboard new models but inference for existing pinned models continues. we also support local eval and logging buffered until connectivity.
[08:36] Derek Liu: ok that's reassuring.
[08:38] Priya Rao: any guidance on subnet sizing for ENIs and ip address exhaustion?
[08:43] Jules Meyer: heavy guidance: reserve at least /23 for production clusters per AZ to have room for ENIs, scaling groups, and PrivateLink ENIs. smaller clusters might be fine with /24 but you risk hitting limits with autoscaling.
[08:58] Amir Khan: our prod is /24 today, we may need to expand.
[09:02] Lena Park: we'll put a migration checklist for subnet expansion.
[09:07] Derek Liu: question on TLS: does Redwood terminate TLS at the PrivateLink endpoint or do we do mutual TLS to the runtime?
[09:14] Marco Ortiz: by default TLS terminates at the endpoint with mTLS between control plane components; for strict setups we support end-to-end mTLS to the runtime.
[09:25] Priya Rao: got it.
[09:27] Amir Khan: any notes about blob storage for models—S3 vs EFS vs local disk for shards?
[09:33] Jules Meyer: S3 is easiest and performant for us; we also support pre-staging to EFS or local NVMe for cold start improvements. large models benefit from local NVMe at the cost of ops.
[09:47] Derek Liu: how do you handle corrupted shard retries?
[09:50] Marco Ortiz: downloader verifies checksums and retries from alternate mirror endpoints; we can pin mirrors to your NFS if you prefer.
[09:58] Priya Rao: about metrics—can we get token-level cost breakdown?
[10:02] Lena Park: yes console shows per-request token counts, GPU time, and cost estimates; we'll share a sample export.
[10:10] Amir Khan: would love to run a perf test with a replay of our production traffic.
[10:14] Marco Ortiz: we can replay traces with synthetic traffic; please share a scrubbed request histogram and we'll simulate.
[10:21] Priya Rao: let's talk schedule— security review, then pilot, then scale. timeline expectations?
[10:28] Lena Park: typical: security review 2 weeks, pilot 2-4 weeks, scale plan 1-2 weeks after pilot.
[10:35] Derek Liu: who owns the pilot infra changes?
[10:38] Lena Park: Redwood helps provision the runtime artifacts and provides runbook; your infra team will make subnet & route changes—we'll support via SE pairing.
[10:46] Amir Khan: ok. can we capture some edge-case network logs—like tcpdump sample—when you hit our NAT?
[10:51] Marco Ortiz: yes, we'll include sample tcpdump snippets and expected socket patterns in the runbook.
[10:59] Priya Rao: great. any competitor callouts? we've looked at Anthropic's on-prem offering and some managed vendors.
[11:08] Marco Ortiz: we try to keep port counts and surface area minimal compared to some managed hosts; we'll include a table of differences.
[11:16] Lena Park: quick note— we've seen customers forget to open route53 resolver inbound rules for PrivateLink; that kills resolution for the control plane names.
[11:26] Amir Khan: noted.
[11:29] Lena Park: any final questions before we list next steps?
[11:33] Priya Rao: not yet. just want to confirm the pilot will simulate our NAT timeouts and path MTU variations.
[11:40] Jules Meyer: yes, we'll run both and share results.
[11:45] Derek Liu: and share the ENI/subnet sizing doc.
[11:48] Marco Ortiz: docs and diagrams we'll push to the folder - link will be in follow-up.
[11:53] Lena Park: perfect. thanks all.
[57:30] (meeting end)
